newsitem.title: ITALY: No end seen yet for cereal price volatility-FAO.
newsitem.headline: No end seen yet for cereal price volatility-FAO.

text.p: A rollercoaster ride in world cereals prices in 1996 may have eased, but instability is not over yet, the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation said on Wednesday.

"During the next few years, while countries adjust to the new policy regime, international cereal prices are likely to be more unstable than at a later stage when the system has settled down," FAO's Committee on Commodity Problems said in a paper to an international grains meeting.
The current grains market could be described as still in disequilibrium and on an adjustment path towards a new market development.
Wheat prices hit record highs and maize and barley prices almost doubled during an extremely volatile 1995-96 season.
In a marked departure from normal seasonal patterns, grain prices did not fall after January and only began to decline with the new crop in June 1996.

FAO said it was hard to assess how much the Uruguary Round, which introduced global rules for trade in agricultural produce and a gradual reduction in subsidy spending and volumes by major exporters for six years from 1995-96, contributed to volatility.

"While the initial stages of trade liberalisation under the Uruguay Round could have some price destabilising effects due to the potential reduction in stocks, trade liberalisation in the longer run should probably have a stabilising effect," it forecast.
More than 50 cereals exporting and importing nations met at FAO's Rome headquarters for the Intergovernmental Group on Grains. The meeting, held every two years, runs until Friday.

"The spike in international grain prices during the 1995-96 season could be regarded as a short-run reaction to a tight market where stocks were drawn down to levels not seen since the food crisis of the mid-1970s," the FAO paper said.
"The single most probable reason behind the recent instability in grain prices is related to stocks," it said.
FAO added that global cereal stocks seemed "unlikely to recover to anything like the level seen in the middle-late eighties".
